name: EC Merger Regulation
impact_assessment: none (2002 recast proposal predates impact assessments; Green Paper COM(2001) 745)
evidence_rating: moderate: peer-reviewed causal studies (event study, sector panels) and a large merger-case dataset, mostly on the predecessor regime or specific sectors; Commission evaluations are procedural and its savings estimates are ex-ante self-assessments
summary: The Merger Regulation set no measurable targets. The Commission estimates its competition enforcement saves customers EUR 12-21 billion a year, about 60% from merger control, but that figure assumes every decision was right. Independent studies find that blocking deals removes expected market-power gains while conditions on approved deals work only partly, that four-to-three mobile mergers raised prices about 16%, and that market concentration in Europe has risen; the 2021 evaluation also admitted some takeovers of innovative start-ups escape review, and the Court of Justice struck down the Commission's fix in 2024.

indicators.objective: The recast proposal (COM(2002) 711, following Green Paper COM(2001) 745) predates the financial-statement indicator system and set no quantified targets. Article 1(4)-(5) required a Commission report on thresholds and referrals (delivered as COM(2009) 281)
Prevent concentrations that significantly impede effective competition (SIEC test)
indicators.indicator: Avoided price increases / reversal of market-power gains
indicators.evidence: Mixed. DG Competition estimates EU enforcement saved customers EUR 12-21bn a year (2012-2025), about 60% from merger control, but this is an ex-ante calculation that assumes decisions were correct. Independent event-study evidence (Duso et al. 2011) finds only prohibitions fully reverse anticipated market-power rents; remedies only partly. Cross-country evidence (Genakos et al. 2018) shows 4-to-3 mobile mergers raised prices ~16%, and concentration in EU antitrust markets has risen since 1995 (Affeldt et al. 2021).
indicators.sources: Verouden et al. 2026; Duso et al. 2011; Genakos et al. 2018; Affeldt et al. 2021

indicators.objective: One-stop shop and efficient case allocation via referrals
indicators.evidence: 2021 evaluation: referral mechanisms 'generally served their objectives well', avoiding many parallel national reviews; 2009 report found thresholds and referrals broadly effective.

indicators.indicator: Share of cases under simplified procedure; burden on parties
indicators.evidence: 2021 evaluation found the 2013 simplification package increased use of the simplified procedure and reduced burden, without quantified savings in the executive summary.

indicators.indicator: Below-threshold acquisitions of innovative/nascent firms ('killer acquisitions')
indicators.evidence: 2021 evaluation found some cross-border deals involving low-turnover innovative firms escaped review; the Commission's response (accepting Article 22 referrals of deals below national thresholds) was annulled by the Court of Justice in Illumina/Grail (3 Sept 2024). Academic evidence on killer acquisitions is US-based (pharma: 5.3-7.4% of acquisitions).
indicators.sources: SWD(2021) 66/67; CJEU C-611/22 P; Cunningham et al. 2021

literature.citation: European Commission (2021), Evaluation of procedural and jurisdictional aspects of EU merger control (executive summary SWD(2021) 67), SWD(2021) 66
literature.title: Evaluation of procedural and jurisdictional aspects of EU merger control (executive summary SWD(2021) 67)
literature.method: review (public consultation, deal-activity research, enforcement data)
literature.headline: Turnover thresholds plus referrals 'generally proved effective'; but some acquisitions of nascent and innovative firms (digital, pharma, biotech) escaped review; referral mechanisms served one-stop-shop aim well; 2013 simplification reduced burden
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's evaluation found the merger rules generally capture the deals that matter and simplification cut red tape, but acknowledged that some takeovers of promising start-ups slip through.
literature.quality: self-evaluation; did not assess substantive outcomes

literature.citation: European Commission (2009), Report on the functioning of Regulation No 139/2004, COM(2009) 281
literature.title: Report on the functioning of Regulation No 139/2004
literature.headline: Jurisdictional thresholds and referral system broadly functioning; at least 240 cases reviewable in two or more Member States in 2007; stakeholders suggested further streamlining of Article 4(5) referrals
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's five-year review found the rules on which authority reviews which merger broadly worked, though some deals were still reviewed in several countries.

literature.citation: Verouden, Bovin, Ilzkovitz, Giacalone & Deisenhofer (DG Competition) (2026), Estimating customer savings generated by competition enforcement in the EU, Competition Policy Brief 1/2026, European Commission
literature.authors: Verouden, Bovin, Ilzkovitz, Giacalone & Deisenhofer (DG Competition)
literature.title: Estimating customer savings generated by competition enforcement in the EU
literature.method: ex-ante calculation (OECD method: avoided price rise x turnover x duration)
literature.headline: EC enforcement generated direct customer savings of about EUR 12-21bn per year over 2012-2025; merger control accounted for about 60% of savings and 63% of interventions; explicitly not an ex-post evaluation and assumes decisions were correct
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's own economists estimate that blocking or fixing harmful mergers saves customers several billion euros a year, but the method assumes every decision was right.
literature.quality: self-assessment; assumptions not tested ex post
literature.interested_party: Authored by Commission (DG Competition) staff assessing their own enforcement

literature.citation: Duso, Gugler & Yurtoglu (2011), How effective is European merger control?, European Economic Review 55(7), 980-1006
literature.title: How effective is European merger control?
literature.method: causal: event study (stock-market reactions at announcement and decision, large EU mergers 1990-2002)
literature.headline: Only outright prohibitions completely reverse the rents measured at merger announcement; remedies only partially, more effective in Phase I than Phase II; the Commission appears to learn over time
literature.summary_plain: Stock market evidence suggests EU merger control fully removes expected market-power gains only when it blocks deals; conditions imposed on approved mergers work only partly.
literature.quality: covers predecessor Regulation 4064/89; relies on market-efficiency assumptions

literature.citation: Genakos, Valletti & Verboven (2018), Evaluating market consolidation in mobile communications, Economic Policy 33(93), 45-100
literature.title: Evaluating market consolidation in mobile communications
literature.method: causal: panel regression with fixed effects (33 OECD countries, 2002-2014)
literature.headline: A hypothetical 4-to-3 merger raises end-user prices by about 16% on average and investment per operator by about 19%; effect on total industry investment not significant
literature.summary_plain: Mergers that cut the number of mobile operators from four to three raise phone bills by about 16%, while total network investment does not clearly rise.
literature.interested_party: Valletti later served as DG Competition chief economist (2016-2019)

literature.citation: Affeldt, Duso, Gugler & Piechucka (2021), Market Concentration in Europe: Evidence from Antitrust Markets, DIW Discussion Paper 1930 / CESifo WP 8866
literature.title: Market Concentration in Europe: Evidence from Antitrust Markets
literature.method: descriptive and correlational (20,000+ antitrust markets in 2,000+ EC merger cases, 1995-2014)
literature.headline: Concentration in EU antitrust markets is at least ten times higher than industry-level measures suggest and has risen over time; strict past merger enforcement is associated with lower concentration, more so in 1995-2004 than afterwards
literature.summary_plain: Using the Commission's own merger files, researchers find markets in Europe are far more concentrated than thought and have become more so; tougher merger enforcement goes with lower concentration.

literature.citation: Cunningham, Ederer & Ma (2021), Killer Acquisitions, Journal of Political Economy 129(3), 649-702
literature.title: Killer Acquisitions
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences on drug development projects after acquisition
literature.headline: 5.3-7.4% of pharmaceutical acquisitions are 'killer acquisitions' that discontinue overlapping drug projects, often below antitrust notification thresholds
literature.summary_plain: Some pharmaceutical takeovers are made to kill off rival drugs, often in deals too small to be reviewed - the problem behind the EU's Article 22 debate.
literature.quality: US evidence; informs EU threshold debate

literature.citation: Court of Justice of the EU (2024), Illumina v Commission (Joined Cases C-611/22 P and C-625/22 P), Judgment of 3 September 2024
literature.authors: Court of Justice of the EU
literature.title: Illumina v Commission (Joined Cases C-611/22 P and C-625/22 P)
literature.headline: Commission cannot accept Article 22 referrals from Member States lacking jurisdiction under national law; annulled Commission decision on Illumina/Grail; the Court noted threshold-based systems cannot catch every problematic deal
literature.summary_plain: Europe's top court ruled that the Commission overstepped by reviewing a deal below all national thresholds, closing the main route it had chosen to catch 'killer acquisitions'.
